problems.title: Sorted Divergence Pair Sum

statement.description:
Given a 1-indexed array of integers telemetry_readings that is already sorted in non-decreasing order, find two numbers such that they add up to a specific target_discrepancy integer.

Return the indices of the two numbers, 1-indexed, as an integer array [index1, index2] of length 2.

You may not use the same element twice. Exactly one valid solution exists.
statement.output_format: list[int] of length 2 containing 1-based indices [index1, index2]

examples.explanation: telemetry_readings[2] + telemetry_readings[3] = 12 + 19 = 31. Since the problem requires 1-based indices, the result is [3, 4].
telemetry_readings[0] + telemetry_readings[3] = -10 + 5 = -5. The 1-based indices are [1, 4].

constraints: telemetry_readings is sorted in non-decreasing order
Exactly one solution is guaranteed to exist

pattern_clues: Array is already sorted in non-decreasing order, which gives monotonic sum properties
Asked to find a pair summing to target without using an element twice
Comparing pairs at both boundaries allows pruning an entire row or column of search space in O(1)

brute_force.approach: Exhaustively check all distinct index pairs (i, j) with i < j using nested loops until the pair summing to target is found.
brute_force.why_it_is_too_slow: Quadratic O(N^2) time complexity evaluates up to 1.25 billion iterations for N = 50,000, causing a Time Limit Exceeded.

optimal_solution.approach: Initialize two pointers at the minimum (left) and maximum (right) extremes. Because the array is sorted, if their sum is too small we must increment left; if too large we decrement right. This converges in O(N) single-pass time.
optimal_solution.why_this_works: The sorted invariant guarantees that for any left pointer, if telemetry_readings[left] + telemetry_readings[right] > target, no element before right could possibly sum with left to reach target, eliminating right permanently.

subgoals.explanation: Place left at index 0 (smallest value) and right at len - 1 (largest value).

subgoals.title: Converge inward based on sum comparison
subgoals.explanation: Evaluate current pair sum; conditionally advance left or retract right.

subgoals.title: Return 1-based indices or terminal fallback
subgoals.explanation: Return [left + 1, right + 1] upon exact equality, or empty list if exhausted.

Initializes left pointer at the start of the array corresponding to the minimum value.
Initializes right pointer at the final index corresponding to the maximum value.
Continues while pointers do not collide, ensuring we never pair an element with itself.
code_lines.risk_note: Strict inequality left < right is required; left <= right would illegally reuse a single index.

code_lines.why_this_line: Computes sum of the two boundary values in O(1) time.
Checks if current sum matches the target discrepancy exactly.
Converts 0-indexed positions to 1-indexed positions as required by the specification.

Increments left pointer to increase the sum because all other values paired with left are smaller than right.
code_lines.risk_note: Incrementing left is the only way to increase the sum monotonically.

Decrements right pointer to decrease the sum because current right is too large for any valid left.

recommended_tests: Target is exactly double an existing element (e.g. array [1, 3, 5], target 6)

recommended_tests: Solution found at index 0 and 1 (output must be [1, 2])

problems.title: Bidirectional Partition Balance

statement.description: You are given an array of package weights weights and an integer threshold representing the maximum capacity of a shipping container. Each shipping container can carry at most 2 packages at the same time, provided the sum of their weights does not exceed threshold.\n\nReturn the minimum number of shipping containers required to carry all packages.

examples.explanation: Container 1: (1, 2), Container 2: (2), Container 3: (3). Total 3 containers.
Each item must be shipped in its own container because no two items sum to <= 5. Containers: (3), (3), (4), (5).

pattern_clues: Each container holds at most 2 items, which maps directly to pairing extremes
Greedy heuristic: the heaviest remaining package must ship; pairing it with the lightest available package maximizes container efficiency
Sorting the weights allows inward pointer convergence from extremes

brute_force.approach: Sort weights. For each unassigned heaviest package from right to left, scan all remaining unassigned packages to find the heaviest partner that fits within threshold. Mark both as visited and increment container count.
brute_force.why_it_is_too_slow: Scanning remaining items repeatedly takes O(N^2) time in the worst case, timing out for N = 50,000.

optimal_solution.approach: Sort the weights in non-decreasing order. Use two pointers left = 0 and right = len - 1. In each step, the heaviest item (right) must be shipped. If the lightest item (left) can share the container, advance left. Always decrement right and increment containers.
optimal_solution.why_this_works: If the lightest available item cannot pair with the heaviest item, no other item can pair with the heaviest item either. Therefore the heaviest item must go alone. If it can pair, pairing it with the lightest is always globally optimal.

subgoals.explanation: Evaluate if lightest fits with heaviest; advance left conditionally and decrement right unconditionally.

problems.title: Fixed Telemetry Window Peak Average

statement.description: You are given an integer array data_stream consisting of n elements, and an integer window_size.\n\nFind a contiguous subarray whose length is equal to window_size that has the maximum average value and return this value. Any answer with a calculation error less than 10^-5 will be accepted.

examples.explanation: Subarray [12, -5, -6, 50] has sum 51, and average 51 / 4 = 12.75.
Single element subarray has average 5 / 1 = 5.0.

pattern_clues: Problem specifies a contiguous subarray of fixed length window_size
Adjacent windows of length k share k - 1 elements in common
Maintaining rolling sum avoids re-summing k elements for each position

brute_force.approach: Iterate through all possible starting indices i from 0 to n - window_size, and sum window_size elements data_stream[i:i + window_size] from scratch using a loop.
brute_force.why_it_is_too_slow: Recomputing the sum of window_size elements for each of the (N - K + 1) windows takes O(N * K) time, which takes up to 10 billion operations for N = 100,000 and K = 50,000.

optimal_solution.approach: Compute the sum of the first window_size elements. Then slide the window from index window_size to the end of the array, adding the incoming element data_stream[i] and subtracting the outgoing element data_stream[i - window_size] in O(1) time.
optimal_solution.why_this_works: When a window moves right by 1 index, only two elements change: the leftmost element leaves the window and a new rightmost element enters. Maintaining the running sum in O(1) per step achieves strict O(N) total runtime.

subgoals.explanation: Sum first window_size elements to bootstrap rolling window state.

subgoals.title: Slide window across remaining stream
subgoals.explanation: Update sum in O(1) by adding incoming and subtracting outgoing element; track maximum sum.

subgoals.title: Compute and return maximum average
subgoals.explanation: Divide maximum accumulated sum by window_size.

Calculates the sum of the initial window of length window_size in O(K) time.
Initializes maximum sum tracker with the first window sum.
code_lines.risk_note: Must initialize with first window sum, NOT 0, to handle all-negative arrays correctly.

code_lines.why_this_line: Slides the window across the remaining elements from index window_size to n - 1.
Adds new incoming element data_stream[i] and subtracts exiting element data_stream[i - window_size] in O(1).
code_lines.risk_note: Off-by-one trap: outgoing element index is i - window_size.

code_lines.why_this_line: Checks if current sliding window sum exceeds historical maximum sum.
Updates maximum sum with new peak window sum.
Divides optimal sum by window_size once at the end to minimize floating point operations.

Instead of recalculating the sum from scratch each time, add the element that just entered the window and subtract the element that just left.

statement.description: Given a string data_packets, find the length of the longest substring without repeating characters.\n\nA substring is a contiguous non-empty sequence of characters within a string.
statement.output_format: int representing length of longest unique substring

examples.explanation: The answer is "wke", with the length of 3. Notice that "pwke" is a subsequence and not a substring.
The answer is "b", with the length of 1.

constraints: data_packets consists of English letters, digits, symbols and spaces

pattern_clues: Looking for the longest contiguous substring meeting a condition (uniqueness)
When a duplicate character appears at the right boundary, the window becomes invalid
Advancing the left boundary directly past the duplicate restores validity in O(1)

brute_force.approach: Check all possible substrings data_packets[i:j + 1]. For each substring, insert characters into a set; if the set size equals substring length, all characters are unique, so update max length.
brute_force.why_it_is_too_slow: Generating and checking all O(N^2) substrings takes O(N^3) time, taking trillions of operations for N = 100,000.

optimal_solution.approach: Use a sliding window [left, right] and a hash map last_seen mapping each character to its most recent index. As right advances, if character was seen at index >= left, jump left to last_seen[char] + 1. Update last_seen[char] = right and max_len = max(max_len, right - left + 1).
optimal_solution.why_this_works: Jumping left directly past the previous occurrence skips all intermediate invalid windows in a single step, ensuring right moves forward exactly N times without backtracking.

problems.title: Minimum Bounded Sum Sliding Frame

statement.description: Given an array of positive integers energy_readings and a positive integer target_threshold, return the minimal length of a subarray whose sum is greater than or equal to target_threshold. If there is no such subarray, return 0 instead.
statement.output_format: int representing minimal valid subarray length, or 0

examples.explanation: The subarray [4, 3] has the minimal length 2 with sum 7 >= 7.
The sum of all elements is 6, which never reaches target_threshold 11.

pattern_clues: All elements are positive integers, ensuring monotonicity: expanding right strictly increases sum; shrinking left strictly decreases sum
Asked for minimal length meeting a sum constraint
Dynamic sliding window where we expand right to satisfy the condition, then shrink left to minimize length

brute_force.approach: For each starting index i, iterate j from i to n - 1, computing running sum. As soon as sum >= target_threshold, record j - i + 1 as candidate minimal length and break inner loop.
brute_force.why_it_is_too_slow: Quadratic O(N^2) worst-case time requires up to 10 billion operations when no subarray or only the full array reaches the target.

optimal_solution.approach: Maintain a sliding window [left, right] and a running current_sum. Expand right and add energy_readings[right]. Whenever current_sum >= target_threshold, record minimal length right - left + 1, subtract energy_readings[left], and advance left until sum falls below target. Return 0 if min_len was never updated.
optimal_solution.why_this_works: Because all numbers are positive, current_sum is strictly monotonic with respect to window boundaries. Both left and right advance at most N times, leading to 2N total pointer steps and O(N) total runtime.

statement.description: Given a binary array binary_signals and an integer max_flips, return the maximum number of consecutive 1s in the array if you can flip at most max_flips 0s to 1s.

examples.explanation: Flip the two 0s at indices 4 and 5 to produce [1, 1, 1, 0, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 0] with 6 consecutive 1s from index 5 to 10.
Flipping 3 zeros from index 5 to index 11 creates a contiguous run of 10 ones.

pattern_clues: Equivalent to finding the longest contiguous subarray containing at most max_flips zeros
Contiguous subarray constraint on a sequence points directly to sliding window
Expand right and count zeros; when zeros exceed max_flips, shrink left until zero count is valid

brute_force.approach: Check all subarrays [i..j]. For each subarray, count how many 0s it contains; if zero_count <= max_flips, update the maximum length with j - i + 1.
brute_force.why_it_is_too_slow: Quadratic O(N^2) time requires up to 10 billion operations for N = 100,000, causing a timeout.

optimal_solution.approach: Maintain a window [left, right] and count zero_count of zeros in the window. Advance right: if binary_signals[right] == 0, increment zero_count. While zero_count > max_flips, if binary_signals[left] == 0, decrement zero_count, and increment left. At each step, update max_consecutive = max(max_consecutive, right - left + 1).
optimal_solution.why_this_works: Each element enters the window via right and leaves at most once via left. Both pointers move monotonically forward, guaranteeing O(N) total operations.

problems.title: Complement Value Index Lookup Table

statement.description:
Given an array of integers sensor_metrics and an integer target_balance, return indices of the two numbers such that they add up to target_balance.

You may assume that each input would have exactly one solution, and you may not use the same element twice.

You can return the answer in any order.
statement.output_format: list[int] of length 2 containing 0-based indices [i, j]

examples.explanation: sensor_metrics[1] + sensor_metrics[3] = 7 + 11 = 18, so return [1, 3].
sensor_metrics[0] + sensor_metrics[1] = 3 + 3 = 6, so return [0, 1].

pattern_clues: Input array is unsorted, making two-pointer inward convergence impossible without O(N log N) sorting
Looking for a pair summing to target: value_A + value_B = target => value_B = target - value_A
A hash map can store previously visited elements and their indices for O(1) complement lookup

brute_force.approach: Use two nested loops to check all distinct index pairs (i, j) with i < j. If sensor_metrics[i] + sensor_metrics[j] == target_balance, return [i, j].
brute_force.why_it_is_too_slow: Quadratic O(N^2) time evaluates up to 5 billion pairs for N = 100,000, timing out.

optimal_solution.approach: Iterate through sensor_metrics once while maintaining a hash map seen_indices mapping value -> index. For each value, compute complement = target_balance - value. If complement is in seen_indices, return [seen_indices[complement], index]. Otherwise, store seen_indices[value] = index.
optimal_solution.why_this_works: Checking whether a complement exists in a hash table takes O(1) average time. Inserting each element after checking prevents an element from pairing with itself and guarantees a single pass.

problems.title: Energy Vault Multi-Step Elevation Climb

statement.description:
You are climbing an energy staircase. It takes total_steps steps to reach the top.

Each time you can either climb 1 or 2 steps. In how many distinct ways can you climb to the top?

Must achieve O(N) time with O(1) auxiliary memory.
statement.output_format: int representing total distinct climbing combinations

examples.explanation: There are three ways to reach the top: 1 step + 1 step + 1 step, 1 step + 2 steps, 2 steps + 1 step.
The 8 combinations correspond to Fibonacci(6) = 8.

pattern_clues: Optimal substructure: reaching step N can only happen from step N - 1 (with 1 step) or step N - 2 (with 2 steps)
Overlapping subproblems: ways(N) = ways(N - 1) + ways(N - 2), exhibiting Fibonacci recurrence
State depends only on previous 2 numbers, allowing O(1) rolling space optimization

brute_force.approach: Use pure recursive branching: def climb(n): if n <= 2: return n; return climb(n - 1) + climb(n - 2).
brute_force.why_it_is_too_slow: Exponential O(2^N) time branches recursively into 2^45 (over 35 trillion) calls, causing a severe Time Limit Exceeded.

optimal_solution.approach: Recognize the recurrence ways(n) = ways(n - 1) + ways(n - 2) with base cases ways(1) = 1 and ways(2) = 2. Use two rolling integer variables prev2 and prev1 initialized to 1 and 2, updating iteratively from step 3 up to total_steps.
optimal_solution.why_this_works: Each state depends strictly on the two immediately preceding values. Maintaining two variables eliminates an O(N) array allocation while calculating the solution in a single linear pass of N iterations.

subgoals.title: Handle base cases
subgoals.explanation: Return total_steps directly if total_steps <= 2 (1 step has 1 way, 2 steps have 2 ways).

subgoals.title: Initialize rolling state variables
subgoals.explanation: Set prev2 = 1 (step 1 ways) and prev1 = 2 (step 2 ways).

subgoals.title: Iterative transition loop
subgoals.explanation: Iterate from 3 to total_steps, computing curr = prev1 + prev2 and shifting rolling variables.

subgoals.title: Return total distinct paths
subgoals.explanation: Return prev1 holding total ways to reach top.

Iterates from step 3 through total_steps inclusive.

code_lines.risk_note: Recurrence relation adds ways to reach from 1 step below and 2 steps below.

Shifts curr into prev1 for the next step.

hardest_lines_to_test.why_it_is_tricky: Failing to guard small steps causes loop range(3, 2) to skip, returning incorrect uninitialized values.
Reversing assignment order (prev1 = curr before prev2 = prev1) overwrites prev1 before prev2 gets its value.

hints: How many ways are there to reach step 1? 1 way. Step 2? 2 ways (1+1 or 2).
To reach step 3, you either take 1 step from step 2, or 2 steps from step 1. So ways(3) = ways(2) + ways(1).
Do you need an entire array to store all previous answers? Only the last two values are ever needed!

problems.title: Non-Adjacent Security Node Optimizer

statement.description: You are planning to harvest energy from a street of security nodes represented by an array of non-negative integers node_capacities. Adjacent nodes have security interlocks: if two adjacent nodes are harvested on the same night, an alarm triggers.\n\nReturn the maximum amount of energy you can harvest without alerting security.
statement.output_format: int representing maximum harvested energy sum

examples.explanation: Harvest node 0 (2), node 2 (9), and node 4 (1). Total energy = 2 + 9 + 1 = 12.
Harvest node 0 (2) and node 3 (2). Total energy = 2 + 2 = 4.

pattern_clues: At each node i, we face a binary choice: harvest node i (yields node_capacities[i] + optimal(i - 2)) OR skip node i (yields optimal(i - 1))
Non-overlapping independent subproblems exhibit the House Robber recurrence: dp[i] = max(dp[i - 1], dp[i - 2] + val)
State only depends on the previous two maximums, allowing O(1) space optimization

brute_force.approach: Use recursive backtracking to explore all 2^N subsets of non-adjacent indices. For each node, either take it and recurse on i + 2, or skip it and recurse on i + 1. Return the maximum yield.
brute_force.why_it_is_too_slow: Without memoization, the recursive tree branches into O(2^N) states, which overflows the stack and hangs for N > 30.

optimal_solution.approach: Maintain two rolling variables prev2 and prev1 representing maximum energy harvestable up to i - 2 and i - 1. For each node, compute curr = max(prev1, prev2 + node_capacities[i]), then shift prev2 = prev1 and prev1 = curr.
optimal_solution.why_this_works: The decision at node i depends only on whether skipping (prev1) or taking (prev2 + val) yields a higher total. By preserving the optimal decision for the previous two subproblems, we find the global maximum in linear time with O(1) memory.

subgoals.title: Handle base cases
subgoals.explanation: Return 0 if empty; return single element if len is 1; return max of first two if len is 2.

subgoals.title: Initialize rolling subproblem trackers
subgoals.explanation: Set prev2 = node_capacities[0] and prev1 = max(node_capacities[0], node_capacities[1]).

subgoals.title: Iterate through nodes with take-or-skip decision
subgoals.explanation: From index 2 to end, compute curr = max(prev1, prev2 + val) and advance rolling state.

subgoals.title: Return optimal harvest total
subgoals.explanation: Return prev1 holding global maximum energy.

problems.title: Word Ladder Shortest Transformation Sequence

statement.description:
A transformation sequence from word begin_word to word end_word using a dictionary word_list is a sequence of words begin_word -> s1 -> s2 -> ... -> sk such that:
- Every adjacent pair of words differs by a single letter.
- Every si for 1 <= i <= k is in word_list. Note that begin_word does not need to be in word_list.
- sk == end_word.

Given two words, begin_word and end_word, and a dictionary word_list, return the number of words in the shortest transformation sequence from begin_word to end_word, or 0 if no such sequence exists.
statement.input_format: begin_word: str, end_word: str, word_list: list[str]
statement.output_format: int representing number of words in shortest transformation sequence, or 0

examples.explanation: One shortest transformation sequence is "hit" -> "hot" -> "dot" -> "dog" -> "cog", which is 5 words long.
The end_word "cog" is not in word_list, therefore there is no valid transformation sequence.

constraints: begin_word, end_word, and word_list[i] consist of lowercase English letters
All words in word_list are unique

pattern_clues: Shortest path in unweighted state space (words are graph nodes, single-letter edits are edges)
Level-order BFS ensures the first time end_word is reached, it is via the shortest sequence
Generating next words by substituting 26 letters takes O(26 * L) per word instead of comparing against all N words

brute_force.approach: Use recursive backtracking DFS exploring all valid single-letter word transitions in word_list, maintaining a visited set to find the path with minimum word count.
brute_force.why_it_is_too_slow: Backtracking explores factorial O(N!) word permutations, causing a severe recursion timeout for lists of thousands of words.

optimal_solution.approach: Convert word_list to a hash set words for O(1) removals. If end_word not in words, return 0. Use BFS with collections.deque storing (current_word, depth), starting with (begin_word, 1). For each word, try replacing each character with all 26 lowercase letters. If neighbor in words, remove it from words (marking visited) and enqueue (neighbor, depth + 1). If neighbor == end_word, return depth + 1 immediately.
optimal_solution.why_this_works: By mutating each of the L character positions across 26 letters, finding valid neighbors takes O(26 * L) instead of comparing against all N words (O(N * L)). Breadth-first search guarantees the first time end_word is encountered, depth is minimal.

subgoals.title: Endpoint validation and word set setup
subgoals.explanation: Convert word_list to hash set; return 0 immediately if end_word is absent.

subgoals.title: Initialize BFS queue with begin word
subgoals.explanation: Initialize FIFO queue with (begin_word, 1) where 1 is the starting sequence length.

subgoals.title: Expand single-character variations and traverse
subgoals.explanation: Pop word; try all 26 letter replacements per position; enqueue match and remove from set to prevent cycles.

subgoals.title: Return zero on unreachable target
subgoals.explanation: Return 0 if queue empties without reaching end_word.

Iterates through each character position in current word.

Constructs candidate neighboring word with 1-character difference.
Checks if candidate word exists in dictionary in O(1).
Removes word from set immediately upon enqueuing to prevent cycles and duplicate visits.
code_lines.risk_note: words.remove() acts as the visited set, saving memory and preventing cycles.

code_lines.why_this_line: Enqueues neighboring word with incremented sequence length.
Returns 0 if end_word could not be reached.

hardest_lines_to_test.code: if end_word not in words: return 0
hardest_lines_to_test.why_it_is_tricky: If end_word is not in word_list, the algorithm would spin through the entire queue before returning 0.

hardest_lines_to_test.why_it_is_tricky: Forgetting to remove next_word from words allows endless cycling between words like "hot" <-> "dot".
